== Biography ==

Mr. McGregor is the proprietor of an enclosed vegetable garden. He maintains it with his wife, Mrs. McGregor, and it is well-planted with lettuces, French beans, radishes, and parsley.

The garden has earned a fearsome reputation among the local rabbit population. Peter's father met with an accident there, after which he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor. This tragic history makes McGregor's garden a place that prudent rabbits are warned to avoid.

== Personality ==

McGregor is a man of strict principle and vigilant property. His garden is a domain he guards with unwavering firmness; any intrusion upon it is met not with warning or second chances, but with swift and forceful response. He does not merely own the garden—he actively defends it, maintaining its status as a place where his will holds absolute sway.

He is a man who acts decisively when his boundaries are crossed. When trespassers enter his garden, he does not hesitate or deliberate; instead, he moves at once with forceful determination, his response sharp and authoritative. His sternness is demonstrated through swift action, without mercy or consideration for the transgressor's youth or vulnerability.

McGregor shows no leniency to those who violate his rules. The very mention of his name is enough to warn creatures away from his property, a testament to the gravity of the consequences that await trespassers. He is a figure of consequence in his community—one whose authority is absolute within his own domain, and whose displeasure is not to be courted lightly.

His nature is as unbending as his defense of his property. McGregor does not compromise, and offers no forgiveness when his boundaries are crossed. He is a man of fixed conviction, steady in his purpose and relentless in the protection of what belongs to him. This stern, unforgiving disposition shapes his reputation and his standing among all who live in the neighbourhood.

== Trivia ==

McGregor's vegetable garden flourishes with a variety of produce, including lettuces, French beans, radishes, and parsley, attesting to his methodical care. His property is marked by a gate that serves as a distinct boundary between his domain and the surrounding countryside.

He is notably protective of his plot, employing a rake both as a practical gardening tool and as a deterrent against unauthorized entry. This dual purpose reveals a farmer's pragmatic approach to both cultivation and protection.
